CA: 3M4EPrHdBxxRDCb8q2RTDQ3oDTi3QGi3iMgVxifqpump

T800 is a pumpfun launch on Solana, barely a minute old at our signal, and the sharpest thing about it is the name: the AI robot from the Terminator films.

There is no story yet beyond that name, and no posts to build one from. Nothing on X mentions this contract, and the T800 ticker pulls in no same-name noise from other tokens.

Attention is absent rather than scattered. No account is talking about it, so there is no big handle to weigh and nobody with a following behind it.

Since our signal the pair has been busy: buys outnumber sells and volume this hour, $38.6K, is larger than the whole market cap. It is still on the pumpfun bonding curve, 73% of the way to graduation, and the market cap has given back ground since our signal.

Mint and freeze authority are renounced, taxes are zero, there is no honeypot, and liquidity sits with the pumpfun program with no LP tokens to pull. The risks are in the crowd: the top ten wallets hold 22.5%, and 62 bundler wallets still hold 36.6% of supply. Of the hundred largest buyers, 41 have fully exited.

The deployer is on its first token, counting this one, so there is no prior record to judge it against. The dev wallet still holds a small slice and has sold none of it.

Smart money is thin. Three smart wallets bought at our signal for $280 in total, the first within seconds of launch. Our own watch list shows nothing, and our verified set is empty: no wallets, no consensus, no lead. No KOL wallets bought either.

The most basic test SemiAnalysis applies to a GPU cluster health check is whether it could possibly work on paper. Several could not.

"We've been through a few of these clusters where there's no way it could possibly work. These are health checks so bad they're worse than no health checks, because they're actively interfering with jobs."

"On Amazon HyperPod Slurm, the first time we tested, there was a health check that needed the node to be healthy before it could run. It could only run once the node was back in the fleet, and it was needed to bring the node back into the fleet."

"There are probably five or ten examples of this throughout testing where the health check never had a chance. It makes you wonder whether these people are really putting it through the paces before they hand it off to customers."

@chigrl From AI. If not now, when?

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at 283.8 million barrels as of the week ending September 25th — the lowest since October 1982, and only about 40% of its 714 million barrel capacity.
It’s been draining since March, when the U.S. committed 172 million barrels to a coordinated IEA release after the Strait of Hormuz closed. DOE expects it to bottom out around 243 million once that commitment is fully delivered, and the next EIA update comes Wednesday.
One thing worth knowing: this release was structured as emergency exchanges, not sales — companies borrow the crude now and owe it back later with a premium. So the barrels aren’t gone forever, but the reserve is still thin while Hormuz stays contested.

items.text:
Before OpenAI became one of the biggest AI companies in the world, Elon Musk was one of the first people to actually buy the hardware it needed.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang recalls announcing an early AI supercomputer in 2016 and getting almost no interest. Musk was the exception.

Musk had requested the system for the nonprofit AI venture he had helped launch with others in 2015, which would become OpenAI.

Huang says he personally delivered the system to the group.

I find this story fascinating because it captures a very different moment in AI.

OpenAI wasn't yet a commercial giant. Generative AI wasn't a mainstream industry. The enormous compute race we see today had barely begun.

Yet Musk was already thinking about the importance of AI infrastructure and securing the compute needed to build advanced systems.

The companies and technologies that now dominate AI were once just small groups trying to get enough hardware to start.

Sometimes, the early decisions look ordinary until you see what they eventually became.

most robot benchmarks are already dead the day they launch.

models memorize the test set. scores look great. real generalization does not move.

@axisrobotics and @openroboto shipped a different thing. Open Axis Benchmark locks a fresh task set every round, pulled from a live Axis library of 6,000+ tasks and 5.5M+ trajectories. the test keeps moving, so you cannot just overfit it.

same engine behind the training loop. browser demos go in, the model decides what is still useful, next collection targets the gaps. they call it letting the model guide the data.

one result from that loop: Embodied RSI took a deployed policy from 22% success to 52% by training the next version on its own real rollouts. expert models on single tasks hit near 100% for about $5 to $10 of compute.

items.text:
Model Distillation vs Quantization - since a ton of people don't know the difference.

Model distillation is one of the most interesting AI tradeoffs:

Take a huge, expensive model.
Teach a smaller model to imitate it.
Lose a little capability.
Gain a lot in speed and cost.

Distillation = teach a smaller model to behave like the bigger one.

Quantization = keep the same model, but represent its weights with fewer bits.

Distillation compresses behavior.
Quantization compresses precision.

Both make AI cheaper to run.

But in very different ways.

Hope this helps.

South Korean authorities are investigating what appears to be a coordinated cyber campaign targeting the country's financial sector.

Confirmed affected organizations currently include:

* Shinhan Bank
* KB Kookmin Bank
* Hana Bank
* BNK Busan Bank
* Hyundai Capital

Authorities say the SAME ATTACKER IP infrastructure was identified across multiple incidents.

The attacker also repeatedly rotated IP addresses while continuing attacks.

More unusually:

Investigators found evidence suggesting AI tooling may have been used to automate attacks against multiple financial institutions at scale.

According to Korean financial-sector investigators, traces associated with:

ARTEX AI

were found in infrastructure used against banks.

ARTEX AI is described as an open-source LLM-based autonomous penetration-testing system.

However:

⚠️ This DOES NOT establish who conducted the attacks.

The tool is publicly available, attacker infrastructure spans multiple countries, and attribution remains under investigation.

The compromises reportedly targeted comparatively overlooked external systems, including:

* Employee support portals

* Internet-facing web services
* Systems missing authentication controls

Attackers reportedly installed malware in at least some cases and stole log files containing customer information.

Authorities say there is currently NO indication that internet/mobile banking systems were compromised or that direct financial losses occurred.
